name: Mehrgarh culture
title: The story of the Mehrgarh culture

text: More than 7,000 years ago, people at Mehrgarh in Pakistan were among South Asia’s first farmers.
They grew wheat and barley and kept sheep, goats and cattle.
src: the founding of the village is now given as either c. 7000 or c. 5250 BCE / The Kacchi Plain of Balochistan, Pakistan / Mehrgarh is one of the earliest known places in South Asia where people farmed
farmed barley and wheat and herded sheep, goats and cattle

text: They built mud-brick houses and stored grain in buildings called granaries.
They even drilled living people’s teeth, the oldest such tooth care known.
src: They built houses of unbaked mud brick, most with four internal subdivisions, stored their grain in granaries
Eleven molar crowns from nine adults buried at Mehrgarh had been drilled during life: the oldest evidence of its kind, taken as a sign of a long tradition of proto-dentistry

text: Later they made shiny beads, pots painted with patterns, and clay figures of women.
Sea shells and lapis lazuli stone came to them from far away, through trade.
src: In Period II glazed faience beads were produced / Togau pottery with geometric designs / The oldest ceramic figurines in South Asia come from Mehrgarh / Until Period VII all were female
Sea shells from distant coasts and lapis lazuli from as far away as present-day Badakhshan / more beads of Badakhshan lapis lazuli in Period II point to long-distance trade

text: A copper charm shaped like a wheel, about 6,000 years old, is the oldest known lost-wax casting.
src: A wheel-shaped copper amulet about 6,000 years old is the oldest known example of the lost-wax technique

text: More than 4,000 years ago, in the days of the Indus Valley Civilisation, people left Mehrgarh.
About 32,000 objects found there tell of thousands of years of village life.
src: Sometime between 2600 and 2000 BCE, when that civilisation was in its middle stages, the site seems to have been largely abandoned
about 32,000 artefacts have been collected / Over thousands of years its villagers moved from a Neolithic life without pottery
